text: Good evening. Welcome to our January 14th, 2025 Board of Supervisors meeting. We are appreciative of you being with us tonight. If you are giving public comments, they will be given from the lectern in the back. For everyone who is watching the live stream of tonight's meeting on the county website, you can participate remotely in the public hearings and public comment portion of the meeting.

Go to the Board of Supervisors webpage at henrico.us forward slash supervisors. Click on Guidance for the Board of Supervisors meeting and scroll down and click on WebEx event. And a moderator will let you know when it is your time to speak.

Speakers will address their comments to the board and will begin by stating their name and address. Discussions between speakers and members of the audience will not be allowed. Speakers who have brought printed documents to share with the board are asked to give them to a sheriff's deputy.

The documents will be included in the record of the meeting. Please stand as we recite the Pledge of Allegiance together and be led in our invocation prayer by Stephen Boots, chaplain for Henrico County Police Division.
Pledge of Allegiance to the flag of the United States of America, to the republic. Father, we thank you so much for an opportunity we have to be here tonight.

Thank you so much for your goodness to us and for a new year that you've given us here. I do thank you that you brought us through the crisis that we dealt with last week. I do pray for those that are going through the wildfires and the situation out in Los Angeles. I pray that you just protect them and keep them safe as well.

And I do thank you for all of those that are being appointed to the positions tonight. I thank you for their willingness to serve in those positions. I pray that you would help them as they do that. I pray for our board as well and for our county manager. I pray that you give them wisdom as they make decisions for this county. I pray that you give us a great year.

Again, we thank you so much for the privilege of being able to be a part of this. I do ask for protection for our first responders, for our police officers, and our firefighters, and those that are doing that work. And again, we thank you for all that you do for us in Jesus' name. Amen.
Andrew, approval of minutes.
Mr. Chair, we have a request for approval of minutes from December 17th, both the regular and special, December 17th, 2024, both regular and special meetings, sir. Is that a motion? So moved.

Motion made by Mr. Smith, seconded by Reverend Cooper. All in favor say aye. Aye. Thank you. Mr. Chair, members of the board, members of the audience, I want to take a minute and recap the events of last week for the members that are here today and those that are watching online.

I'm going to take my time for a minute and just relay exactly what we know happened, when it happened, and there's more that is coming out regarding the water crisis that our county experienced last week.

There will be a briefing to the Board of Supervisors on February the 11th with our 30-day post-op, if you will, that was committed to on Saturday by members of the board, myself, to the residents of the county.

And you'll hear about those efforts. But going back, if you recall, it was Sunday, January the 5th. Our county actually opened our emergency operations center. We didn't do it for water. We did it because we were making sure that all winter storm plans and needs were addressed for snow because we had snow that we were dealing with.

And little did we know that that emergency operations center would actually not close until Saturday, January the 11th. So we went from January the 5th to January the 11th. January the 5th, we pretreated and plowed thousands of lane miles of road for snow.
Then as we moved into this water crisis, our call center answered almost 8,000 calls. Our teams through pods throughout the county distributed more than 153,000 cases of water.
We made available 120,000 gallons of potable water through 20 tankers. We made deliveries to 48 daycares, 900 separate residences that needed assistance, and 11 assisted living facilities.

More importantly, we had hundreds of employees and even more community and volunteers from our school system working, yes, 24 hours a day to meet the needs of our community during this crisis. I want to thank all of the employees and also members of the board that were also delivering water and seeing what individual residents that may have needs, how they could be addressed.
I want to begin by thanking Terrell Hughes, our Director of Public Works, for how we handled that snow, not just on January the 5th, but also this past weekend.

And then especially give thanks out to Bentley Chan, the Director of Public Utilities, for navigating an issue and his work crews. This issue, I want to underscore, and perhaps double and triple underscore, was not of our creation.

Our Chief of Emergency Management and Workplace Safety, Rob Rowley, guided us and supported our agencies partners through all of these events. So that snowstorm that closed our schools and led to flooding and a loss of power at the city's water treatment facility, that will be a conversation I think this region is going to be having for many days and weeks ahead. The disrupted water service in our county, this disrupted water service in the county because Henrico and Richmond

share the region's water resources under an agreement that dates back several decades. So with the city's plan out of commission, our residents started losing water late Monday, and those problems worsened through Tuesday. At its peak, we had more than 24,000 of our customers without water. We needed to act. We proactively disconnected from the city's water system and thought that we could route water across the county from our treatment facility on three-chopped road that proved extremely difficult because the system was simply not

designed to do that working in frigid weather our crews crisscross the county making careful adjustments to valve after valve in our water system and ultimately we were able to restore 6 000 additional homes by taking that approach those efforts however were further complicated by a water main break that we had in sandstone we declared a local emergency that you'll hear the board act on tonight but not lift which allowed us to act quickly and we began providing bottled and potable water to impacted communities on wednesday as the city's pumps began to

re-pressurize the system with the assistance of henrico and hanover the virginia department of health issued a boil water advisory for eastern henrico that was inevitable that we that was the second day that we did not have water moving through the system and we recognized that and And we needed to issue a similar advisory countywide because we really can't be 100 percent certain where all of the water goes that comes in from the city of Richmond.

Again, our water system and Richmond's are connected. By late Thursday, service had been restored to our neighborhoods and pressure was strong enough for us to begin the series of water quality tests. Then finally, Saturday morning, our test results were clear, and we were able to lift the advisory.

Now, the story does not end there. As promised, Saturday, Enrico County has already hired and released two outside firms, and they are Whitman, Recwart, and Associates, WRA for short, and Aqualaw, to complete analyses of all aspects of our utility system and response.

The scopes of the reports include a timeline of events, evaluation of infrastructure, let me say that again, evaluation of infrastructure, and recommendations on how to make our system, particularly in the eastern portion of the county, more resilient, and contractual agreements that we have in place with other local governments.

Additionally, the county will be completing an after action on our community response and public communications. As noted in my comments as I began, that report will be presented to the board on February the 11th, which is exactly 30 days after it was after Saturday's briefing.

However, these reports, I want to assure the residents of the county and actions will be the first of many. The underlying question, particularly from our central and eastern residents and businesses, is how will the county become more reliant on our system?

This question, quite frankly, cannot be sufficiently answered in 30 days. So we are going to take a little more time in getting that answer, but I think that 30-day review is going to give us an early indication as to how that may be possible.

It will take many years and millions of dollars to put into place all of the components necessary to make our system more resilient. Now, as I close, I don't want to give anyone any false assurances regarding the reliability of the city's water treatment plant.

That water treatment plant continues to come back into operation, and there are many, many things that need to happen over the next week for that operation to be fully functional and reliable. That is the information that we have.

We are going to continue to pump out information, reliable information, as soon as we have it for all of our residents. But right now, we are up and running, and I did want to comment on that timeline. And once again, thank the members of the board for their particular actions and the Herculean effort of the staff that I saw working so hard last week.

Mr. Chair, I have no other comments unless you have anything for me. Do you want to have anyone, is there anyone here that could speak to the earthquake? I do see messages. We see stuff on social media, so I don't want to put anybody on the spot.

But we did have an earthquake in Henrico. It was in, so earlier today while the board was in work session, there was an earthquake in Hanover County. We believe in northern Ashland is the information that we got.

But if you heard a loud boom, that's what that was. It was an earthquake in Ashland. And right now we don't have any information regarding any damage to any county homes or buildings. But we'll definitely be going through that assessment.

Thank you, sir. All right, colleagues, do we have any comments? Mr. Chair, I have a comment. And I would ask Ms. Kay Alfario to please approach the podium. So, as some of you may know Kay, she is the president of the Cultural Arts Center at Glen Allen and serves very diligently and passionately in that role, and I've enjoyed getting to know her.

But last month, and the reason I asked her to be here today is last month, she was integral and part of a Christmas program at the James River Juvenile Detention Center, and I was able to attend as well as a couple others of us there.

And it was very personally touching to me because I have, some of you may know, I work with juveniles who are court involved. And I have some children that are in the James River Juvenile Detention Center. And so to be able to watch them participate in a normal event and to be kids and to, you know, show their talents and to put down their guards was incredibly moving to me.

So, that was one part, but even better than that, I think, is a program that they have been working on wherein they have brought artists to work with the children to be able to commission pieces. I was able to, and they were for sale, and I asked staff to bring them down for me, and I wanted to show them off here today.

These are done by our young people, two young ladies, I believe it was, that painted these two with the help of staff brought over from the Cultural Arts Center, and they were for sale. And so I was able to purchase these two, and this is money that is saved for these young people, and they go into their bank accounts, and they're able to use it to get a fresh start.

But even more than the money, I dare say, you know, when I told these young ladies that I had bought their works, they were really beside themselves. and they couldn't believe that folks believe in them the way that they do. And these are the types of works that we do and folks that work with our folks in the county do that we don't often get to brag about.

And so I really just wanted to be able to share what was being done last month and give Kay an opportunity to speak to us from her heart about it as well. Thank you. And it is very near and dear to my heart. And we could not do what we do without the support of the County of Henrico.

I am constantly amazed, consistently amazed at the way you guys govern with both integrity, with honesty, and with real caring. I think that, you know, Mr. Batokas, you talked about all the people that came out for the water crisis. It's because of the way you guys lead.

It's because you don't forget, in the midst of all of the things you have to do, you don't forget about the humanity of it all. And you remember the people. And that's what you did for us. And James River is very near and dear to my heart. We got this idea several years ago.

My first, I remember sitting in Reverend Nelson's office and saying, we have an idea. We want to do something at James River. We believe that art can make a difference in the lives of these kids. And we really want to try this program. And thanks to your support, my next step was Mr. Patokas' office to say kind of the same thing.

And you guys were so supportive. And you have been with us every step of this program, and it has made a difference. I am absolutely amazed at the difference that this is making in these kids' lives. Seeing that they can recognize their worth and they find a voice through their art is just amazing.

I love going to the third floor, even though I have to have somebody let me in up there. I love going to the third floor. When you take a left out of the elevator, there's a wonderful painting on the wall. That was done by one of the youth at James River. It was the first painting he ever painted.

He had never painted anything before. He worked on it for months, and we were just so proud. And when the county purchased it, it made his day. He was already out, but he got the money for it, and it's made a big difference. At the event that you were talking about, we do a couple of art shows every year where we invite people to come in.

We put the art on display and sell it. I'm very excited to say that 17 artists combined made over $4,000 in the sale in one day. Yeah, I bought one, too. I couldn't help myself. But that's just the kind of thing that is making a difference.

And at least three of the kids came up to me afterwards, and they were amazed that the county manager, that some of the supervisors were all there to see them. It just was, it amazes them that people that are important, that are people they would never meet, in their daily lives would come to see them, and it makes a huge difference.

So that's been big. We have – I just found out today that the kids from the program have been invited to go to the Governor's Mansion to meet. They've also – they've been to several – they've had several opportunities to come to shows at the center where they can meet with the performers afterwards.

But, you know, it's talking to the individual kids. It's the young man who said to me one day, you know, before I learned to draw, if I got mad, I just wanted to fight. And now I've realized that if I draw, I'm not mad anymore. There's the young man who I bought a painting from.

He was doing it. He said he wanted to learn to paint for his daughter. I bought the first painting he had ever painted. And when I learned what he wanted to do, I offered to give it back to him so he could give it to his daughter. I said, you can have the money, but I'll give it back. And he said, what would you do with it? I said, well, hang it in my office. And he was amazed. He said, people will see it.

And I said, yes. And he said, you keep it. I'll get my daughter another one. So it is making a difference. They're really getting involved. And we have plans to continue. We have plans to grow. I met with the people from James River today.

We are, thanks to Ms. Roundtree, we have connected with the first poet laureate of Virginia, who is going to start a poetry program out there. We hope that will culminate in the kids not only being able to have their first experience sitting in a theater, but have their first experience on stage actually performing.

We're going to look at improv classes. We already have music classes going on, but the improv is going to teach kids to listen to each other, to cooperate, and to verbalize, and to really express themselves. So we're very excited about that. We also have a program in the works to do a music recording, teach them how to record their own music, write and record their own music.

So we have big plans for the future, and we couldn't, again, do it without you all. And I would just like to close by saying that at the end of the program, we went into the pods to see where the kids had decorated their living quarters. And one of them, in one of the pods, one of the young men had gotten out and unfortunately had committed suicide the week before, so it prompted a lot of discussion.

And as they were working on their art projects, they started to talk, and they had a big – they had created a sign. And what they talked about was the fact that there is hope in the world, and they have hope. And they said that to them, hope stands for hold on, pain ends.

So this is the kind of impact you guys are having, and I just cannot thank you enough. Thank you for your support. We will continue to try to make you as proud as we possibly can by making as big a difference as we can. Thank you. Mr. Chair, I apologize for the breach in protocol.

We do have notice now from the U.S. Geological Service, the epicenter of the earthquake that was noted earlier. Earthquake was magnitude 2.8. It was 7 kilometers north of Wyndham, just inside the Hanover County line.

Chair, so this is the first meeting of 2025, the organizational meeting. First item on the agenda is agenda item 1-25, and this is the election of chair.

So here you're going to see our county attorney, Andrew Newby, come forward to conduct the election of the chair for the Board of Supervisors for the 2025 calendar year. Thank you, Mr. Manager. We will now conduct the election of the chair of the Board of Supervisors for calendar year 2025 and thereafter until his or her successor is elected and qualified.

So we'll now open the nominations. Are there any nominations for chair of the Board of Supervisors? Nominate our current vice chair, Dan Schmidt. Thank you. Is there a second to the nomination of Mr. Schmidt? Are there any further nominations for chair?

Hearing none, I declare the nominations closed. And I will now call for a motion on Resolution 1-25, nominating Mr. Schmidt as chair. Is there a motion? So moved. Is there a second? Second. Any discussion on the motion? Mr. Newby, I would take a moment for discussion here.

And I say this sort of preemptively, recognizing some of the things going on in our region and across the pond a little bit. So when we had the elections of 2023, it did represent a bit of a monumental change for this board.

As I understand it, it's the first time that three new board members came on at the same time in the history of Henrico County. It also represented a flip politically in the board, and it certainly represented a couple of firsts for my particular seat.

And so recognizing that, I think that throughout this year I have carried with me the knowledge that there were many who were elated and excited and had expectations about the results of that election, and others were quite the opposite, were disappointed, dismayed, perhaps even a little bit fearful as to what that would mean, changing the composition of the board. And so I not only carried that through the year, but I carried that into our discussion or into our consideration of the election of the chair this year. So some of you may know that, unlike other jurisdictions,

Henrico sort of has a way of doing elections of chair, and it follows a bit of a loose rotation, which is designed to ensure that folks have opportunities to serve. And that loose rotation over the years has meant, for example, that Reverend Nelson served as chair, I believe it was twice while he sat in the minority politically of this board. And I think that people agreed that that was a good thing. And so as we came up on this, I wanted to have a conversation and discussion with Mr. Schmidt because the way that that rotation worked meant that as vice chair last year,

he was expected or presumed or sort of suggested that he would be chair this year. And I wanted to have a discussion with him because it is a unique situation and I don't ever ignore elephants in the room and I wanted to acknowledge that and and we had a good a good hearty discussion I think and I you know asked him about what his views were for leadership what his views were you know going forward especially with the dynamic that we had what his priorities were and I shared my thoughts on leadership and the dynamic and all of those things and we really weren't weren't that far off with the big picture things.

You know, the fact that, and I will say this, I think it is important to note that I, myself, had no intention, request, thought, aspiration to serving as chair this year. To my knowledge, none of my Democrat colleagues had that aspiration at all.

So it was not a situation as occurred across the pond where there was a bit of that division. So that didn't come into play at all. But I do serve as a Democrat. And what that means is that I am a Democrat because, generally speaking, the values that are important to me, the mores, the priorities, the humanity, as Kay spoke of, those all, in my estimation, align with what I view to be more aligned with the principles of the Democrat Party.

But more so and more importantly than that, when we're serving here at local government, we recognize and I recognize that you all just want us to get things done for all of you and your kitchen table issues, regardless of whether there's an R behind our name or a D behind our name.

And so the question that I had to ask and have to know the answer to is, is there anything about Mr. Schmidt and his services chair that would impact or interfere and impede the goals that I have for the coming year or that I believe my colleagues have?

And I am confident and comfortable after my discussion with Mr. Schmidt that that is not the case. And so, again, I don't say this to belabor it to be overly dramatic, but I recognize that there are questions and people have, again, feelings and thoughts and i wanted to affirmatively state them and address them and so based on that mr newby i do support mr chair for excuse me mr schmidt for chair thank you thank you any further discussion on the motion all right so we have a motion on resolution 1-25 nominating mr schmidt as chair there's been a proper second in discussion all in favor say aye aye all opposed the resolution
passes congratulations mr chair mr schmidt the clerk will now swear in mr schmidt thank you all

i do want to thank you colleagues um because you are the ones who after the residents elect us give us the opportunity to serve. So thank you for allowing me to be the chair last year. It meant a lot to the Verona District and our entire community for allowing me to serve as an elected board member for my fourth term on the Board of Supervisors. It truly, this past year, has been one of the busiest and possibly the most rewarding year of my life professionally.

Please know that for the past 13 years, I've taken this responsibility serving our citizens every day seriously. Last year as chair, I strive for us to communicate and collaborate as a board so that we can build consensus around key issues and articulate a vision for our county's leadership and staff to implement.

I've encouraged us to tell our story, the Henrico story, with transparency and boldness and what a year it was, not even counting last week's extraordinary challenges with our water system, which I'll touch on in a minute.

Last night, I thought back to my first year on the Board of Supervisors, how excited I was, the expectations that I had for myself, and the expectations that others put on me. There were those, and ironically, Misty Roundtree shared these same things in her comments, who thought that my win was a fluke and the county was doomed.

Others who were giddy and excited that both Shannon Taylor and I were the first Democrats that had been elected in a while. Some who thought that because we were elected, new and fresh ideas would flow, and they did.
But I knew that I had worked with a board who had worked together for 16 years. And it was somebody new, young, 25 years of age younger.
I didn't know what to expect. And honestly, they probably didn't either. But each day, each week, each month, and as the years went past, I learned my job and I learned what I was called to do.
There were moments when decisions were pragmatic. There were other moments when thoughts were guided by what we had done. There are many moments when we were challenged to think outside of the box.

What I learned most importantly was how to connect with the community that we were called to serve, the people of Henrico County, the employees who work for Henrico County. I enjoyed my time working with those who came before this current board.

Dave Cackley, Dick Glover, Peto Bannon, Frank Thornton, Tommy Brannon, Courtney Lynch, and my current partner, Steele, Dan Smith. I always thought, even though we disagreed on ideology, that we all thought we were doing what was best for our districts and for Henrico County.

The thing that I appreciated most was what Misty referenced earlier. We respected each other. So much so that the board elected to choose to allow Frank Thornton to serve even when he was the only Democrat on the board. Four Republicans, one Democrat. First African American elected. They didn't look at his ideology or his race. They didn't use that to keep him from serving multiple terms as chair.
Neither did they keep Petal Bannon from serving as the first woman, and technically still, beyond six months, the only woman before Misty Roundtree to serve a full term on the board.

I respect the fact that we respect each other. We have, we are, and we will always look to each other as human beings first before we judge based upon politics. So that led me back to where we were last year with that spirit in mind.

I approached 2024 with extreme optimism. We started with the swearing in of three new board colleagues, Roscoe Cooper of Fairfield, Mr. Roundtree of 3Chop, Jody Rogish of Tuckahoe. You might have expected a board with three newcomers to take a while to jail to have a learning curve before we could get down to the business, but I quickly learned that was not us.

On the 17th day of our first term together, we were standing in the cold on a Verona Riverfront, voting to purchase Verona Farms, more than 2,000 acres of land that represents the birthplace of Henrico County.

I believe that set the tone for a remarkable year. We focused on our young people, engaging, inspiring, and challenging them. Monica Callahan and her team led the second Teen Summit RVA that all of us did the best that we could to support.

Within Ricoh County Public Schools, we launched in Ricoh CARES to strengthen our mental health support systems for students and for families. We approved a budget that reinvested in core services, including schools and student safety.

We advanced our bond projects, provided residential and business tax relief. Our triple AAA bond ratings were reaffirmed, which is another independent confirmation of our outstanding financial management.

We celebrated as a team this summer with events marking both Juneteenth and Independence Day. We continue to enhance our quality of life, modernizing Henrico's first park, Cheswick Park, and opening Taylor Farm Park, which is now the standard for what a local park can be.

We focus on sustainability and protecting our environment. With our heart committee, we reforested parks and school grounds, providing shade and reducing runoff into creeks and streams. We also initiated a project to install electronic vehicle charging stations at more than a half dozen county facilities.

Sports tourism exploded with the first year of activity at the Henrico Sports and Event Center. March brought us the Atlantic 10 Women's Basketball Championship and a record month of hotel revenues. We also hosted our high school graduations and scores of other events with more coming.

I was trying to push Dennis Bickmire to allow me to say we had a half million visitors, but he says it was close to 400,000. We partnered with community organizations to expand the Nova Swim Facility at Regency to improve Striker Park and acquire the Crossings Golf Course, which is being improved as a potential stop on the PGA Tour.

We also have a new championship pickleball complex at Ponce Track Park. For me, one of the most important things that happened this year was establishing a $60 million trust fund to put home ownership within reach of more of our community's workforce.

New affordable homes are already coming to both Verona and Tuckahoe districts, and our fund is attracting attention as a model, a local solution to a national problem. With the city and other partners, we made sure that our region has an emergency shelter during extreme weather.

And with our broadband project, we're making high-speed Internet access universal to Henrico. We created a new Department of Outreach and Engagement to supercharge our efforts to make Henrico a welcoming place for everyone. Construction was non-stop with road projects, like the improved Creighton Road project that borders both Fairfield and Verona.

A new and expanded sidewalks and the Fall Line Trail. We're getting ready soon to open the police's new South Station and Bungalow City Firehouse 23, both in Verona. We work with GRTC to increase residence mobility with expanded transit service north to Virginia Center Commons and the new Link Microtransit Service in Sanston.

I was honored to serve as chair of GRTC on the board with our new chair, Mr. Smith and Todd Ewer. We also passed a critical milestone in efforts to secure our water resources and thus our community's future.

Can't wait for that to come online. In November, we assumed operational control over our massive new reservoir in Cumberland County. To be clear, these are just highlights. You all know we did so much more. We had lots of positives last year.
We also had some challenges, some things that did not work, some things that we tried, that we failed at, but we persevered. I'd like to thank everyone who made 2024 such a success for our county.

Our county manager and his team, our departmental leaders, and all of our hardworking employees. None of this would be possible without such a tremendous team of highly skilled individuals with compassion and a commitment to deliver outstanding public service.

As the outgoing chair, I especially want to thank our residents for believing in us, for trusting us, and yes, challenging us to do better. The challenges we faced last week with our county's and region's water systems are stark reminders that our work continues.

Public service is an active, ongoing exercise. We must plan for better tomorrows, but we also must remain nimble and ready to respond to whatever comes our way. I'm honored to serve. I was honored to serve as chair and incredibly proud of the work that we have done together as Team Henrico. I'm definitely excited that I serve on this board with these four

EHPAP was created by unanimous vote of the previous Board of Supervisors on June 13, 2023. At the April 23, 2024 meeting, when it was reordained, I noted that entitlements, real or perceived, can and usually do rapidly expand beyond their initial scope.

The apparent need to substantially increase the assets limit from $30,000 to $50,000 has quickly proven that point. As was entirely predictable, complaints from employees whose net liquid assets make them currently ineligible seem to be driving the change.
